passage: Some music inspires you to move your feet, some inspires you to get out there and change the world. In any case, it's  {{1}} to say that music moves people in special ways. If you're especially into a piece of music, your brain does something called Autonomous Sensory Meridian Response (ASMR), which {{2}}  to you like a sting in your brain. It turns out that ASMR is pretty special. According to a  {{3}} published study in The Journal of Prevention of Alzheimer's Disease, the part of your brain responsible for ASMR doesn't get lost to Alzheimer's. Alzheimer's  {{4}} to put people into layers of confusion, and the study confirms that music can sometimes  {{5}} lift people out of the Alzheimer's haze and bring them back to (at least a likeness of) normality … if only for a short while. ASMR is powerful stuff! This phenomenon has been  {{6}} several times but rarely studied properly. One of the most famous examples of this is the story of 92-year-old Henry Dryer, who comes out of dementia(痴呆) while listening to songs from his youth. Jeff Anderson, associate professor in Radiology at the University of Utah and {{7}}  author on the study, says "In our society, the diagnoses of dementia are {{8}}  resources to the maximum. No one says playing music will be a cure for Alzheimer's disease, but it might make the symptoms more {{9}}  , decrease the cost of care and improve a patient's {{10}}  of life."
